title: Branded a troublemaker: Granz, George Wein and the $50 offer
summary: After exposing the agency he says Norman Granz and George Wein never hire him; he recalls turning down $50 a night at Storyville, and decided to stay in Paris.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: You see? Now, then, they told me, he says, "That's all right. You'll never work in New York again." So I began to calculate, I said, "Oh, yeah, I guess I'm washed up there." It's still going on today. Because George Wein, I knew him when he was in school, in high school, because his brother -- I worked at a club, his brother was manager, at the [Kitten] Club in Boston, and George, he was about 15 or 16 years old, was still going to high school. But the message got out about Kenny is a troublemaker. So Norman Granz, George Wein, those people, they never hire me, never. But you know, I just laugh at them, you know, because I say, "I need you guys like a hole in the head." If you fellows are paying the slave wages you're paying in America, I can't use it." So to give you an idea, when I was in the States last year, I worked in Chicago with Al Haig, and the boss and I, we talked it over, and he says, "Look, Kenny, I can only give you 250 a night." I said, "Well, don't worry about it." I said, "Well, I'm going to be here anyway, so it's okay." So I finished the job there

at the Showcase and come to New York. So Joe Newman's wife [Rigmor] was running the place for Joe. [Storyville] So you know what they offered me? $50.00 a night. I said no. She said, "Well, everybody gets $50.00 a night." So then was when I learned that it was George Wein owned the place. The Storyville, or whatever it is. $50.00. That's what they offered Kenny, $50.00. She said, "Well, everybody gets $50.00." I said, "Not me." I said, "I wouldn't go around the corner for $50.00, and I've been in Paris 20 years and I've never worked for that kind of money since I've been over there, so I'm not coming back home to work for $50.00 a night." So he sees me in New York -- in Paris, at the Palais de Chaillot, he says, "Well, when you come to New York I'll give you a job." I said, "I don't want a job. I don't need a job. And please don't offer me a job." So that was the end of that. So they never offered me anything. So I'm glad about it, because I --
Well, whatever -- I mean you're so right. Anything they do, it's done just that way.
Yeah, it happened. That's how it all happened, you know. But I just couldn't stand to see Dizzy taken like that, you know. As tight as we were.
As good friends as we were, I couldn't, no. I said I'll die first, but I'm sure going to tell Dizzy what's happening.
And I did. So that kind of washed me up for New York. So, luckily, I came to Paris and I stayed, you know.
